eligibility_reason: MSCE writes L1 trace memory, L2 policy memory, and L3 environmental cognition at run time after each episode (Algorithm 2, 'Upon episode finalization: ... Write traces with V = pending', p. 18) and retrieves that same governed memory hierarchy in later episodes to condition future behaviour ('At inference time, MSCE retrieves memory in three tiers', p. 18); the agent itself authors the store rather than reading a fixed corpus (Section 4.4, p. 6). Published 2026, English, full text available (27 pages) — I2, I3, I4 hold. No exclusion criterion applies: memory writing/retrieval is the paper's central contribution (not E5), an externalised store is written at run time (not E2 or E3), it is an LLM-based agent system (not E6), and it is well over four pages with a full experiments section (not E7).

facets.justification: The contribution list names a three-level hierarchy — 'L1 trace memory stores grounded step-level evidence. L2 policy memory induces recurring procedural patterns... L3 environmental cognition memory abstracts declarative knowledge' (p. 2) — plus a crystallized skill store, and Appendix B.9 states the retrieval mechanism explicitly as tiering: 'At inference time, MSCE retrieves memory in three tiers' with skills tried first, L3 providing priors, and fallback to L1 traces (p. 6, p. 18). The combination/routing across these tiers is itself the paper's framework contribution, not an incidental detail.

L3 environmental cognition is produced by an LLM call over a cohort of policies and traces that is not any single source item ('d ← LLM(Πenv , C, T )', Algorithm 1, p. 17), and skills are crystallized by an LLM from an L2 policy plus evidence into a new callable procedure (Appendix E.5 skill-drafting prompt, p. 25). Step values are also produced via 'reflection-weighted value backfilling', propagating self-reflections ρ into computed trace values V (Eq. 2, p. 6) — generated content not present in the raw trace.

Appendix B.9 (p. 18) states a declared multi-signal combination for both tiers used at inference: skill retrieval is 'ranked by trigger relevance, reliability η, and source-policy gain', and trace retrieval 'combines exact cues such as error signatures with semantic similarity over compact state summaries', with high-value traces prioritized — an explicit fusion of exact/structured matching, similarity search, and a value-based ranking rule.

Evidence is 'Experiments on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo' comparing MSCE against 'state-of-the-art skill-augmented and memory-driven agent baselines' (Abstract, p. 1; contributions list, p. 2). This is a controlled lab comparison on public benchmarks, not a fielded system with real users or deployment consequences, so it is coded validation rather than evaluation.

The stated evidence is comprehensive evaluation over two fixed benchmark suites, EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo, against multiple baselines with reported performance gains (contributions list, p. 2: 'Comprehensive evaluations on EvoAgentBench and LoCoMo show that MSCE achieves state-of-the-art performance'). No manipulated experimental condition against a held control beyond the benchmark/baseline comparison is described in the pages given.

The first item of the contributions list on p. 2 names the contribution as a framework: 'We propose MSCE, a training-free memory–skill co-evolution framework that organizes long-horizon agent experience into grounded traces, procedural policies, and declarative environmental cognition.' Code is released (p. 1, GitHub link), but the paper argues for the architecture/organisation itself rather than the artefact.
